title: Identity and Membership
intro: `in` asks whether something is **inside** something else: `"@" in email`. `not in` asks the opposite. `is` asks whether two names point to the **very same object** — use it to check for `None`. For everyday comparisons of values, use `==`.

questions.prompt: With text, `in` checks for a piece of text anywhere inside. `is None` and `is not None` are the clearest way to test for a missing value.
questions.exampleCode:
result = None
print(result is None)
print(result is not None)
print("@" in "maya@example.org")
print("z" not in "pizza")
questions.explanation: `not in` is one operator: it reads like English and gives the opposite of `in`.

questions.prompt: `email` holds an email address someone typed. Store in `has_at` whether it contains `@`.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert has_at == ('@' in email), 'has_at should be True only if email contains @.'

tests.name: bool
tests.code: assert isinstance(has_at, bool), 'Store the result of the in check itself.'

questions.hint: `"x" in text` is True if the text contains x.
questions.explanation: `in` saves you from searching through the text yourself.
`cat` appears inside the word, but capital `C` doesn't.

questions.prompt: Which is the recommended way to check whether `x` has no value?
questions.explanation: `is None` checks for that exact object. `not x` is also True for 0 or empty text, and `x = None` assigns.

questions.prompt: This should check whether `name` contains a space, but it's a *SyntaxError*. Fix it.
questions.starterCode:
name = "Ana Lima"
has_space = " " is in name

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert has_space is True, 'has_space should be True for Ana Lima.'

questions.explanation: `is` and `in` are separate operators; `is in` isn't Python.

questions.prompt: Passwords may not contain spaces. `password` is set. Store in `no_spaces` whether it has **no** space in it, using `not in`.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert no_spaces == (' ' not in password), 'no_spaces should be True when the password has no space.'
tests.message: Use not in to check for a space.

questions.explanation: `" " not in password` reads almost like English.

questions.prompt: No reply has arrived yet. Fill in the blank so `missing` is `True` when `reply` is `None`.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert missing is True, 'missing should be True.'

questions.hint: Which operator checks for the very same object?
questions.explanation: `reply is None` is True when reply holds None.

questions.prompt: `letter` holds a single lowercase letter. Store in `is_vowel` whether it's one of `a e i o u`, using one `in` check.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert is_vowel == (letter in 'aeiou'), 'is_vowel should be True only for a, e, i, o or u.'

questions.hint: Put all the vowels in one piece of text and check whether `letter` is in it.

questions.prompt: `has_digit` should be `True` only if `code` contains a `1` or a `2`. It's always truthy instead. Fix it.
questions.solution:
code = "ABC"
has_digit = "1" in code or "2" in code

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert has_digit is False, 'has_digit should be False for ABC.'
tests.message: has_digit should be False for ABC.

questions.hint: Each side of `or` needs its own complete `in` check.
questions.explanation: `"1" or …` is just the text `"1"`, which is truthy. Write `"1" in code or "2" in code`.

questions.prompt: A sign-up form gives `email` and `nickname` (which may be `None`). Store `needs_nickname` (True when nickname is None) and `valid_email` (True when email contains both `@` and `.`). Print both like `True False`.
questions.solution:
needs_nickname = nickname is None
valid_email = "@" in email and "." in email
print(needs_nickname, valid_email)

tests.name: nickname
tests.code: assert needs_nickname == (nickname is None), 'needs_nickname should be True when nickname is None.'

tests.name: email
tests.code: assert valid_email == ('@' in email and '.' in email), 'valid_email needs both @ and . in email.'
tests.message: Check email with in and and.

tests.name: output
tests.code: assert __output__.split() == [str(nickname is None), str('@' in email and '.' in email)], 'Print needs_nickname and valid_email.'

questions.hint: Use `is None` for the first and two `in` checks joined by `and` for the second.
questions.explanation: Small, well-named booleans make form checks easy to read.
